summary:
Itamar Friedman, CEO of Qodo (Quality of Development Optimization), asks whether human code review will still be mandatory by end of 2026 and argues the bottleneck has moved from code generation to review and validation. He identifies two engineering philosophies: every line must be human-trusted, or ship bugs and fix them in production for velocity. His central claim is that models are no longer the constraint, since code-review benchmarks stagnated across recent model releases; the missing piece is context, which is scattered across agents.md, cloud.md, and skills.md files, varies between teams, and is combined with MCP/RAG layers that lack governance.

Tribal knowledge sits in senior developers' heads, in documents, and heavily in Slack/Teams threads, and must be codified. Codification must serve two audiences at once: agents need verbose, structured formats, while humans only maintain wiki-style interfaces they like. Qodo surfaces violated rules with links for humans and posts comments addressed to other agents so follow-up agents inherit prior fixes; steadily declining human PR comments signal readiness for automation.

Deeper context encodes system architecture, recent P0 outages, and microservice contracts as a graph where nodes represent services/repos and edges capture contracts and historical root-cause discussions. With that graph, reviewers stop reading one PR in isolation and instead spot collisions across in-flight changes, with automatic approve/block driven by semantic rules rather than free AI choice. Closing the loop requires real-time self-learning context drawn from PR history, accepted and unaccepted reviews, developer discussions, and past production breaks, accumulated where agents can locate it. Friedman reframes the goal as moving from artificial intelligence to artificial wisdom, codifying accumulated judgement into rules, standards, and graph nodes, with Qodo's stated 2027 target of zero critical or high-severity production bugs.

sections.title: Opening: where the bottleneck moved and why code review exists
sections.summary: Friedman polls the room about post-coding bottlenecks and code review as a day-to-day concern. He introduces Qodo (Quality of Development Optimization) and frames the talk around achieving the 'last human code review.' He defines code review's two purposes: validating quality, safety, and architecture; and serving as a final alignment/learning gateway before production.

sections.title: The optionality question and two camps
sections.summary: Friedman asks whether human code review will still be mandatory by end of 2026 and whether developers will still read diffs line-by-line. He recounts meeting engineering leaders at a drone show and identifying two camps: one insisting every line be human-trusted, the other willing to ship bugs and fix them in production for velocity. He notes most teams sit on a spectrum and that the chosen philosophy dictates the tools and milestones needed.

sections.title: Models are not the barrier; context is
sections.summary: Friedman argues models are no longer the constraint. He cites his recent visit to a leading lab where code-review benchmarks barely moved across the latest model releases. With proper context, models reason adequately; without it, they fall back to generic suggestions like 'did you consider error handling?' Today's context is fragmented across agents.md, cloud.md, and skills.md files, varies between teams, and is further obscured by MCP and RAG layers lacking governance.

sections.title: Where context lives and why codification needs two interfaces
sections.summary: Friedman locates tribal knowledge in senior developers' heads, documents, infrastructure docs, and heavily in Slack/Teams threads. Codifying this knowledge means building interfaces for both agents (verbose, structured) and humans (wiki-style), because developers will only maintain formats they like. He shows Qodo surfacing violated rules with links for humans and posting comments addressed to other agents so follow-up agents know which fixes already passed. Fewer human PR comments over time signal readiness for automation.

sections.title: Encoding architecture, contracts, and past outages
sections.summary: Beyond rules and standards, the deeper context is system architecture, recent P0 outages, and microservice contract breaks. Friedman shows a graph where nodes represent microservices/repos, edges capture contracts, and links point to historical root-cause discussions. With that graph in place, automatic approve/block can be driven by semantic rules rather than leaving AI to choose freely, allowing review to shift from reading one PR to spotting collisions across in-flight changes.

sections.title: From reviewing PRs to reviewing the software graph
sections.summary: Friedman argues that approve/block knowledge must itself be accumulated as context, and that software development and code governance will shift from reviewing pull requests to reviewing an entire graph abstraction in which PRs appear as bubbles. Reviewers will see issues across multiple in-flight PRs and the contracts they risk breaking. To reach this future, organizations must codify standards in ways humans can trust, audit, and control, and must build real-time self-learning context drawn from PR history, accepted and unaccepted reviews, developer discussions, and past production breaks. That context must be located where agents can understand how it fits, not merely dumped into files, and must be paired with governance infrastructure for visibility beyond the graph.

sections.title: Infrastructure, gradual automation, and the path to artificial wisdom
sections.summary: Friedman warns that shipping AI-generated code faster than humans can review it means you are inside the problem, not ahead of it; only by gathering context and automating review can teams deliver the promised 10x velocity. He calls for owning rules and standards with analytics on how often each rule is triggered and whether it is still useful, plus full visualization of the software graph to spot in-flight PRs that will collide. Auto approve and auto block must be introduced gradually by adding more blocking and approving rules over time. He closes by reframing the goal as moving from artificial intelligence to artificial wisdom, codifying accumulated developer judgement into rules, standards, and graph nodes that serve both agents and humans. Qodo's stated 2027 target is zero critical and high-severity bugs in production.
